Thanks to /v/trucks and @townbike and @lwuwykwa I was all geared up to bring my D200 home on the back desert highways. Well, everything but extra fuel.

The ride I had lined up had a family emergency. A work associate was heading that way earlier in the day but I couldn't raise the seller in time to get the backup ride. I had already gone and picked up everything for the trip [well, everything but extra fuel] by the time the seller called and offered to drive an hour to come pick me up. Loading my motorcycle on the back of the truck was a no-go because the rack was too probably low, so I took the ride.

On the way up we were discussing the guy's blown out knee, one of the reasons he didn't want to keep the truck. We discussed the economy, another underlying reason - but the clutch was just too tough to use with his knee. After we passed a border checkpoint he busted out some scrip called "green crack" and on my 2nd hit I realized my gun was loaded and I started worrying about what the law was since the weapon was in a holster in the bottom of my toolbag.

I put a new air filter on the truck then promptly stalled the truck backing out. The battery he had didn't seem to be cutting it so he offered me a bigger one out of another car he was selling. I offered him $50 for the battery and we swapped them out.

I knew where there was a gas station on the way back, but apparently I passed the nearest one without recognizing it. So I ran out of gas 7.7 miles from the gas station I knew about. Some guys were working the field with a big John Deer; I tried to make it to where they were parked but not quite. I called the seller and his phone immediately died but he knew I had run out of gas. I started walking.

The day was over at the Chile farm. Walking wasn't bad, actually kind of nice. The ride out to the small town was dodging tumbleweeds and massive dust storms. We had talked about a lot of stuff including Trump and Hillary and Obama. I realized after I gave him the $50 for the battery that I had paid him an extra $100 on the balance of the truck, but since neither of us had counted it carefully there was no hard feelings.

As I passed the first field, passing giant red Chile peppers laying on the shoulder of the highway, I didn't mind walking the 8 miles. But I didn't have to, the shift at the farm was ending and the guys were coming out onto the highway to go home. Thumbed twice and the third truck picked me up.

On the way toward town I told him the story about picking up the truck. These towns are so small he asked the name of the guy I bought it from the next town over, expecting to probably recognize him. He didn't know him. Luis told me that he was going to go get 1/4 of a deer someone had shot but if they didn't need help butchering he would be happy to drive me to get gas and back. I told him I really appreciated the ride, but he didn't need to take me all the way back. I told him I was going to stop and get dinner anyway and I was sure I could get a ride back to the truck, but he wouldn't have it and he handed me a home-made carnitas burrito [one of two that were warming on his dash]

We went to his house to get his knives and dressing tools. I waited outside while his dog barked at me. On the next leg he told me about the dog breaking its last chain and biting some kid on a bike who threw rocks at it. This was potentially a bad situation but he talked it out with the kids parents.

We met up with his friend behind a processing plant and he passed him the knives, then took me offroading to the gas station. I think he just wanted to use the 4x4 on his truck, and he told me the story about getting the truck as we passed the old man's property. The old man didn't have enough eyesight to drive the truck anymore.

I bought him a beer at the gas station. Funnily it was the second beer I had gifted today, my friend who was initially going to give me a ride was distraught because of a death in the family so I had brought her the first beer and some herbal supplements to help her feel better.

We got back to the truck and he showed me how to put gas directly into the carb. But we couldn't get it started. He was spraying starter fluid down the intake and we almost got it started. Then it caught fire.

I threw the round air filter cover down on top but the wind was so high the fire wasn't going out. Luis started to take off his jacket and I stopped him and used mine to cover the gaps. The fire went out and Luis said "no more starter fluid".

We couldn't get the thing started. There was a 68" flat screen on the back of the truck that the seller and I were gonna drop off on the way to town. But we got off task because of swapping the battery out and I was just planning on bringing the TV home and giving it away. Luis had to go, and he gave me his phone number in case I got stuck. I told him I was a special kind of stubborn and I would get the truck home.

Luis left and I looked through my Chiltons to see about replacing the fuel filter. I also kind of thought I might have just flooded it. I put my battery booster on the battery and let it charge so I didn't crank the battery down.

As Luis pulled away, the seller pulled up. I told him we couldn't get it started with starter fluid, and maybe he smelled it but he said "it caught fire huh?"

Then he got in the truck and started it right up. I guess the technique was to rapidly and forcefully pulse the gas pedal because of the nature of the Edelbrock 4-barrel carb.

I made it to the gas station and as I was dumping in all my fluids Luis pulled up with his friend and said "hey you made it!". So we loaded the TV into his truck and I thanked him again for his help. As I opened the hood I noticed someone had dropped a Lipton Green Tea that hadn't been opened in the busy gas station drive. While Luis' friend and I were loading the TV, he asked me the name of the guy who sold me the truck, expecting to recognize it two towns over.

By now it was dark, I got about 3 blocks up the road before I realized the headlights weren't on. Eventually I pulled the connectors off both sealed headlamps and wiped the dirt away and got them going.

I'd like to say I made every stoplight on the way back; I missed one.
